slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open by naming the task: Chapter 4 asks what a line does to a plane once side, crossing, and interior become formal predicates. Ground the deck in the chapter-four notebook and the assigned source span, printed pages 63 through 89 and PDF pages 78 through 104. The lecture should feel like a lab for turning incidence pictures into tests.

slides.label: Chapter Map
slides.notes: Use the map to keep the proof ecology visible. Plane separation starts with a sign or side relation, then upgrades that relation into segment crossing tests, angle and triangle interiors, Pasch-style existence theorems, and finally convexity criteria for quadrilaterals. Emphasize that later theorems are not isolated facts; they are built on reliable side bookkeeping.

slides.label: Side Predicate
slides.notes: Treat the signed equation as the computational version of side. A point not on the line receives a positive or negative label; pairs with matching labels live on the same side, and pairs with opposite labels live on opposite sides. This is an algebraic model of the separation relation, not a replacement for the axioms in arbitrary geometries.

slides.label: Segment Crossing
slides.notes: Push students from point classification to segment behavior. When the endpoint signs have opposite values, continuity in the coordinate model forces an intersection with the separating line. The important caveat is that axiomatic plane separation abstracts the conclusion, so the sign formula is a model for intuition and checking, not the definition in every plane.

slides.label: Notebook Calibration
slides.notes: Use the notebook figure as a calibration image. Ask students to inspect the two color classes first, then locate the separating line and predict which pairs of points would force a crossing segment. The visual target is simple but essential: side labels are relational data, and the line itself is the boundary excluded from either open side.

slides.label: Pasch Crossing Law
slides.notes: State Pasch as the theorem that prevents a line from secretly entering a triangle and never leaving. If a transversal meets one side under the usual nonvertex restrictions, the side bookkeeping forces another side intersection. The figure should be read dynamically: the crossing with AC changes which exit side is available and makes the triangle interior observable.

slides.label: Crossbar Theorem
slides.notes: Move from triangle sides to angle interiors. The crossbar theorem says that a ray placed inside an angle at A must meet the opposite side BC of triangle ABC. The teaching point is not just the intersection; it is that the phrase inside an angle carries enough separation information to force a concrete segment hit.

slides.label: Triangle Interior
slides.notes: Build triangle interior as an intersection of three half-plane choices. A point is inside the triangle when it lies on the same side of each edge as the opposite vertex, avoiding the edge lines themselves. This formulation is useful because it makes interior membership testable one edge at a time and prepares the convexity discussion.

slides.label: Quadrilateral Tests
slides.notes: Use the quadrilateral artifact to shift from triangles to four-sided figures. Convexity can be diagnosed by consistent orientation, positive signed area, and diagonals that remain in the interior rather than escaping outside an edge. The orange diagonals in the figure are not decoration; they are witnesses for how the boundary encloses the region.

slides.label: Pasch Geometry Checklist
slides.notes: Connect the visual tests back to axiomatics. A Pasch geometry is not merely a coordinate plane with familiar pictures; it is a setting where side relations, segment crossings, and interior predicates satisfy enough incidence and separation rules for Pasch and crossbar arguments to run. The checklist helps students separate model-specific calculations from theorem-level assumptions.

slides.label: Proof Dependencies
slides.notes: Use the dependency graph as a proof-roadmap rather than a decorative network. Primitive terms and axioms feed definitions, lemmas, theorems, and checks; model examples sit at the end as stress tests. Ask learners to name which arrow would break if same side were ambiguous or if segment intersection were not guaranteed.

slides.label: Auditable Checks
slides.notes: Treat the numerical records as accountability for the visuals. The notebook checks midpoint betweenness, area calculations, an angle measurement near 68.2 degrees, and nonblank image statistics across four figures. These facts are not the theorem, but they make the computational lesson auditable and help distinguish a mathematical diagram from a pretty picture.

slides.label: Side Arithmetic Exercise
slides.notes: Use the exercise to make students perform the side arithmetic themselves. They should compute signs, classify same-side and opposite-side pairs, and predict which segments cross L before drawing anything. The point is to rehearse the Chapter 4 habit: a spatial claim should become a predicate, and the predicate should decide a crossing or interior question.

slides.label: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the chapter question. A line separates the plane by producing two coherent sides, and those sides support theorems about crossings, interiors, rays, and convex polygons. The most durable takeaway is methodological: in synthetic geometry, pictures guide intuition, but separation predicates are what let proofs move.
